summary: An interpretability study of six frozen diffusion code models (DiffuCoder-7B, Dream-Coder-7B, Stable-DiffCoder-8B, UltraLLaDA-8B, LLaDA2.0-mini, LLaDA-flash). It fits difference-of-means linear probes on pooled residual-stream activations to tell passing from failing MBPP+ attempts at the same problem, then tries to steer generation along the probe direction. Probes read correctness above chance (peak within-problem AUC about 0.67-0.82), but do not consistently beat the model's own confidence. Steering toward 'correct' does not improve pass rates, and steering the other way hurts.

claims.claim: Linear probes distinguish passing from failing attempts in all six diffusion models, with the strongest reads beyond the early layers.
claims.evidence: Figure 2 and Table A1 give peak AUCs of 0.67-0.81 in the original comparison. The reported value is the maximum over layers, chosen on the same out-of-fold scores with no separate layer-selection holdout, so the peaks are optimistic. The Figure 2 curves are 'reconstructed from result summaries' and peak at different layers than the original estimates in five of six models.

claims.claim: Mutation controls show the probe tracks correctness rather than surface style.
claims.evidence: DiffuCoder only: AUC 0.670 on 392 MBPP+ mutants and 0.692 on 334 HumanEval+ mutants, plus 0.774 on mutations of its own code. These are point estimates; the bootstrap procedure is admitted to be invalid (repeated draws merged).

claims.claim: Probes offer no consistent advantage over model confidence.
claims.evidence: Table 1: DiffuCoder probe 0.842 vs negative token entropy 0.838 on only 19 mixed problems (95 attempts); Qwen2.5-Coder probe 0.677 vs log-probability 0.703. The authors explicitly decline significance or equivalence claims.

claims.claim: Steering along the probe direction does not dependably improve generation, while the opposite direction degrades it.
claims.evidence: Fig. 4: pass@1 0.433 baseline, 0.429 random, 0.388 positive probe, 0.298 negative. Table A3 (30 tasks): baseline 15, positive global 14, negative global 5, positive conditional 15, learned direction 5. With 30 tasks, a one-task difference is noise, and repeated untreated bf16 runs had different pass counts. The negative-direction harm (5 of 30) is the only large effect.

patterns.note: Looks at cheap internal correctness signals (probe or token confidence, AUC about 0.68-0.84) as possible verifiers. They are not LLM reviewers, and the paper shows they neither beat output confidence nor repair code. Unit tests remain the label and the arbiter.

methodology.sample: MBPP+ (main) and HumanEval+ (mutation controls). Cohorts per analysis range from 19 to 56 mixed problems (95-448 attempts). Steering uses 30 evaluation tasks.
methodology.baselines: Shuffled-label nulls for probes, ten matched-norm random directions for steering, an untreated generation baseline, and model-confidence scores (token entropy, log-probability).
methodology.models: Six diffusion code models; autoregressive comparisons with Qwen3-Coder, GLM-4.5-Air (SWE-bench-derived rollouts) and Qwen2.5-Coder (MBPP+).
methodology.variance: Five noise seeds for three models in the perturbation study; standard deviation across ten random steering directions. The bootstrap is admitted to be invalid and the permutation test does not refit probes, so there are no valid significance claims.
methodology.ablations: Residual noise, attention-edge removal, steering only at still-masked positions, a learned direction optimized for reference-token log-probability, and final-layer versus normalized-state probes.
methodology.contamination_controls: None stated. MBPP+ and HumanEval+ are old public benchmarks.

standards.peer_review: arXiv preprint (v2); no venue or journal_ref.
standards.artifacts: A project repository and supplementary package with probe and steering scripts, figure data and per-task steering outcomes. Activation arrays, capture helpers and consistently recorded model and dataset revisions are missing, so the model experiments cannot be rerun exactly.

biases.detail: The confidence comparison rests on 19 mixed problems and steering on 30 tasks. Cohorts differ across analyses, so 16-step and 32-step results cannot be compared.
The authors themselves say the uncertainty estimates are miscalibrated (merged bootstrap draws, no refit under permutation, no holdout for layer selection), so only point estimates are reported.
MBPP+ and HumanEval+ are short Python function tasks.
Single-function programming puzzles, unrelated to repository-scale software work.
The reconstructed layer curves disagree with the original peak estimates in five of six models (Appendix A). Repeated untreated steering rows gave different pass counts.

coi.affiliations: Duke University; perseus.so; Efficient Computation Inc.
coi.vendor_products_evaluated: None of the authors' products are evaluated; all models are third-party open weights.
coi.funding: No funding statement in the available text.
coi.detail: A startup affiliation, but the paper reports mostly negative results about third-party models, with nothing to sell.

verdict_reason: Off-topic: this is model-internals interpretability of diffusion language models on Python function puzzles, not software-development practice, codebase discovery, onboarding or any harness decision. On its own terms it is an honest negative result: probes read correctness, do not beat output confidence, and steering does not help. But it rests on 19-30-problem cohorts, layer selection without a holdout, admittedly miscalibrated uncertainty, and reconstructed figures that disagree with the original estimates.
applicability: Does not transfer. A Java team using hosted frontier models through agent hosts has no access to residual-stream activations and would not use diffusion code models. The only loose takeaway is consistent with harness practice: internal or confidence-based 'is this correct?' signals are at best a weak ranking hint (AUC about 0.7-0.84 on toy tasks) and do not repair code, so executable tests and compile checks remain the verifier.
